guest.bio_context: Katrina Mulligan previously served in senior roles at the Department of Defense, National Security Council, and Department of Justice, including as number two at the Pentagon overseeing special operations. She then made the transition to OpenAI, which she describes as the hardest professional transition of her career, moving from one of the most hierarchical organizations on the planet to its exact opposite. Her dual vantage point inside both Washington national security structures and frontier AI development makes her a rare voice on AI policy and government transformation.

context.transcript_excerpt: What if we're asking the wrong question about AI? Everyone is focused on who will build the most powerful technology, but what if the real race isn't about building AI at all? Hi everyone, I'm Lynn Thoman and this is Three Takeaways. On Three Takeaways, I talk with some of the world's best thinkers, business leaders, writers, politicians, newsmakers, and scientists. Each episode ends with three key takeaways to help us understand the world and maybe even ourselves a little better. Today I'm excited to be with Katrina Mulligan. Katrina is head of National Security Partnerships at OpenAI, the company that created ChatGPT. She previously served in senior roles at the Department of Defense, National Security Council, and Department of Justice. She was number two in the Pentagon overseeing special operations. Few people have seen both Washington and frontier AI development from the inside. She joins us to discuss why AI is unlike any technology revolution before it and how it will transform the way we work, compete, and solve problems. Hi, I'm Katrina and thanks so much for joining Three Takeaways today. Excited to be here. My pleasure. Katrina, you have a great quote. You said something like the world is looking at a calendar while OpenAI is looking at a watch. What does that mean? I'll start by saying when I made the move from the Pentagon to OpenAI, it was the hardest professional transition of my career. I think part of why it was so challenging is because I wasn't expecting it to be so hard because I felt like I had had really difficult transitions before, but there was something really different and destabilizing about moving from probably the most hierarchical and bureaucratic part of the most hierarchical and bureaucratic organization maybe on the planet to the exact opposite of it in every way. One of the other disorienting things about the transition was that people measure time differently at OpenAI and time passes differently at OpenAI than anywhere I've ever been. We often say internally that a month at OpenAI feels like a quarter anywhere else. And so once you've hit three months in or four months in, it's like you've been a year anywhere else. And I try to help government understand that by saying frequently that like you're looking at a calendar and we're looking at a watch. It is an indication that the unit of time that we are thinking about that we have ahead of us needs a complete recalibration. And that's because the technology is changing so quickly as well as the opportunities? It is. And it's because, you know, we've long anticipated that eventually the models would get good enough that they would begin to conduct the research that improves themselves. And you know, this idea, which is known in the AI industry as recursive self-improvement is not quite upon us yet, but it's getting really close. And so like I can't even think five years into the future in terms of where this technology will be by then, because it's so impossible. It's so nonlinear at this point, and we're really reaching much more of an exponential. What are other ways that make this AI revolution fundamentally different from every tech revolution before it? The biggest one from where I sit is that this is really the first time in American history that a technology of this consequence is being developed exclusively by the private sector with no government involvement. If you think back to the advent of electricity, nuclear fusion, the internet, the Human Genome Project, GPS, all of those are examples of technologies that were developed with government as a stakeholder in the development of the technology. They had a seat at the frontier table. They may not have been driving the whole thing, but they had at least a finger on the steering wheel. That is not true about AI, and it's really unique in that all the AI labs are operating really independently of government, and government doesn't have a major AI initiative that can in any way compete

pending_qa.q: What makes the AI revolution fundamentally different from every previous technology revolution in American history?
pending_qa.r: According to Mulligan, this is the first time in American history that a technology of this consequence is being developed exclusively by the private sector with no government involvement. Unlike electricity, nuclear fusion, the internet, the Human Genome Project, or GPS — all of which had government as a direct stakeholder — AI labs are operating entirely independently, giving government a different and potentially larger set of blind spots.

pending_qa.q: What is recursive self-improvement in AI and how close is it to becoming reality?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan explains that recursive self-improvement is the idea that AI models would eventually become good enough to conduct the research that improves themselves. She states it is not quite upon us yet but is getting really close, and that because of this nonlinear, increasingly exponential trajectory, she cannot even think five years into the future in terms of where the technology will be.

pending_qa.q: What was the state of ChatGPT when it first launched and what changed to make modern AI so much more capable?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan notes that when ChatGPT was first rolled out there were only 200 people at OpenAI, and the initial model — likely GPT-3.5 — produced what she describes as junior high school level outputs. Two breakthroughs changed this: first, the discovery of scaling laws, showing that multiplying compute and data by 10x produces predictably better model performance; and second, teaching models to use tools and agentic harnesses, enabling them to do search, access emails, navigate document repositories, and perform computer use.

pending_qa.q: Beyond saving time, where is the biggest opportunity for AI in healthcare and scientific discovery?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan cites OpenAI's partnership with a children's hospital, where frontier reasoning models were run against unsolved pediatric cases — patients who had been in the system for years with no diagnosis. The models were able to suggest new pathways, new tests, and new potential diagnoses, resulting in entirely new diagnoses for families who had never received answers. She calls this a model for what is possible when organizations are willing to creatively explore rather than remain in a defensive crouch.

pending_qa.q: What is the single biggest predictor of a successful AI transformation in an organization according to OpenAI's implementation experience?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan says the biggest predictor is the extent to which the C-suite personally uses AI in their own work. A bottom-up approach of simply giving everyone access to the tool is necessary but insufficient; leaders at the very top must be getting reps and sets themselves, because, as she puts it, you do not get fit by reading about working out.

pending_qa.q: What is a 'model garden' and why does Katrina Mulligan consider it a mistake in AI adoption strategy?
pending_qa.r: A model garden is the practice of making 12 to 20 different AI models available in a single place so employees can choose among them. Mulligan argues this is expensive, creates unnecessary friction for general users, and provides no material benefit — noting that a typical HR employee does not need 12 choices when typing a query into a chatbot. She predicts organizations will look back on model gardens as a poor use of effort and resources.

pending_qa.q: How does China's approach to AI differ from the United States, and could America build the best AI and still lose?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan identifies three key differences: China has much higher public trust in AI, the Chinese government and CCP have a more direct seat at the frontier AI table compared to the U.S. government, and China has moved faster to recognize AI as an infrastructure play and make strategic investments accordingly. She explicitly answers yes — America could win the race to AGI on the technology side and lose it on adoption, because developing-world societies are integrating AI far more openly and quickly.

pending_qa.q: How far ahead is the United States from China in AI development, and is that lead secure?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan estimates the U.S. has opened up its lead to a single-digit number of months — approximately six to eight months ahead, up from roughly four to six months previously. She stresses that this lead is far from guaranteed, that China has impressive and talented engineers who are determined to win, and that the U.S. must approach the competition with the same seriousness China does.

pending_qa.q: How should government change the way it funds and thinks about AI to unlock its full potential for public services?
pending_qa.r: Mulligan argues that government must stop funding AI purely as an IT line item and begin allocating resources to real, sizable programs of record targeting substantive mission problems. She specifically envisions AI transforming citizen-facing services — from the DMV to tax preparation — so that each interaction becomes slightly more positive, creating a cumulatively very different experience of government over the course of a year.

pending_qa.q: What are Katrina Mulligan's three key takeaways on AI for government and national security leaders?
pending_qa.r: Her three takeaways are: first, AI is no longer a future policy question but core infrastructure for public service and national power; second, trust is the rate limiter and organizations must move beyond a defensive crouch on the trust question; and third, the real opportunity is redesigning work, not simply adding a chatbot to old processes.
